rows.evidence: Q1: Section 3 (Case analysis), Fig. 7, Fig. 9, Tables 3-4 <U+2013> the authors report their own experiment in a 13 ha jujube orchard in Alar City, Xinjiang (2021), comparing yields, yield-estimation accuracy and harvest economics across six schemes.
rows.notes: The study does not use soil sensors or monitor soil moisture, and does not report any irrigation adjustment or its effect on fruit quality. Space information is collected by agrometeorological satellites (temperature, moisture, precipitation, wind etc.) and a DJI UAV (crop images, terrain). Its own results are: (i) a yield increase in 1 ha under the proposed full-process management versus traditional management (Fig. 7, no numbers or mechanism given); (ii) UAV-based yield estimation accuracy of ~90-95 % (Fig. 9, Table 5); (iii) ~12 % higher economic benefit from harvest path planning with integrated space information (Table 3), where the 'quality' difference (average selling price) is attributed to harvest timing relative to weather, not irrigation. 'Real-time' data use is described only for technicians developing field management programs from cloud-uploaded UAV/satellite data (Section 2.2), with no soil moisture sensing. The claim about soil-sensor-driven irrigation adjustments is therefore not supported by this study's own evidence.

notes: Full text appears complete. The paper is a jujube-orchard case study of UAV/satellite information integration for field management, yield estimation and harvest path planning; it contains no soil sensor, soil moisture measurement or irrigation treatment.
